newsitem.title: USA: Cadillac sees 1997 sales over 190,000 units.
newsitem.headline: Cadillac sees 1997 sales over 190,000 units.

text.p: The general manager for General Motors Corp's Cadillac motor car division said Monday he expected sales for the 1997 calendar year of just over 190,000 units, up about 20,000 from 1996.
John Grettenberger, the outgoing general manager of the division, said Cadillac sales would include the first full year of the Cadillac Catera, which is aimed at younger luxury car buyers.
Catera brand manager Dave Nottoli said he expected North American sales for the car to exceed 25,000 in 1997.
"We feel real confident we will be able to sell in excess of 25,000 units," Nottoli told reporters following a Cadillac presentation at the North American International Auto Show.

Nottoli said Cadillac would be receiving data on Catera buyers at the end of the month. It would then be better able to tell if the car is attracting the younger drivers GM hopes will add new life to the aging Cadillac brand.
But Grettenberger said his intitial input from dealers was that about 50 percent of Catera sales were made to new Cadillac drivers, higher than about 25 percent he had initially expected.
"We're starting to attract some people here now that we weren't talking to at all before Catera," Grettenberger said.
Nottoli said Cadillac is looking to sell Catera in Lebanon and is also exploring the possibility of selling the car in Taiwan.
Such a move would be consistent with efforts to position Cadillac as a global brand.

Grettenberger said sales in Japan and the Far East are expected to continue to rise, after Cadillac posted sales of just over 3,000 in Japan in 1996, while efforts are also being made to strengthen European distribution channels.
The company also will introduce a new version of its Seville model, with right-hand drive, at the Tokyo auto show in the fall.

Cadillac also said Monday it would offer its StabiliTrak stability control system on all front-wheel drive models in 1998. The system, which uses two sensors that make 50 to 60 diagnostic decisions every 1/100 of a second to help prevent a car from spinning out, is currently available on only three 1997 models.
